[0:08] This means I can do things like have multiple different agents from different providers review my code, and I can even get them to debate each other.
[0:15] If you've ever tried to combine multiple models from different providers, you know how frustrating that can be.
[0:20] You become the bottleneck because you're copying and pasting responses between sessions, you're switching between different applications or terminal windows,
[0:28] or you have to implement complex workflows or implement hooks to get all of this working.
[0:34] It can be extremely frustrating.
[0:36] This is omnigent and it's open source. [...] [12:12] Now, depending on the app that you're building, Poly will actually just delegate the work with three different sub-agents because this game is so simple.
[12:20] It's just kicking off one agent, this guy over a year.
[12:24] And this is using Opus 5 to do the implementation.
[12:27] And again, because the plan is so detailed, pretty much any model, including Opus 5, would be perfect for doing the implementation.
[12:35] What's good to know as well is that Onigent does include browser automation, so the agent will be able to test and screenshot the
[12:42] app and make any improvements if it runs into any bugs.
[12:46] So a lot of the coding harnesses we're used to will allow you to fork the conversations and maybe swap out the models. [...] [13:32] Either way, I hope you enjoyed this video.
[13:34] I want to thank Omnigent for sponsoring this video, and I'll leave a link to Omnigent in the description of the video, which will tell them that I sent you.
[13:42] If you enjoyed this video, hit the like button and subscribe to my channel for more agenda coding tutorials.
[13:47] I'll see you in the next one.
[13:50] Bye-bye.

# Building a harness for open models

16 min read

A model that “forgot” the task may have been shown mostly stdout. A model that uses the wrong tools may have been given a transcript where compaction rewrote the goal into something vague. And a model that seems “slow” may be running in a harness that adds the current time to the system prompt on every turn, breaking cache reuse.

I know that last one a little too well.

Most popular agent harnesses were built around closed frontier models. Closed models have huge context windows, a lot of recovery ability, and a pretty generous token budget, so a lot of harness bugs never surface. You can be sloppy with the environment and the model bails you out. [...] But a lot of the time, the harness is making the task much harder than it needs to be for the model. This issue is exacerbated in harnesses that were tuned around a frontier model. I’ve personally seen this with Claude Code and open models (especially local ones).

I have been building agent loops around open models for a while now, and each model seems to have its own way of exploring, using tools, and getting unstuck. I call it the model’s essence. I see this as the model’s working style. It can usually be observed in the traces of a harness. You get to see what the model is fighting and what it enjoys doing. [...] At the same time, open-weight models have gotten much better at coding and agentic work. GLM-5.2 feels like a recent example of that shift becoming harder to ignore. It is obviously not a model you’ll run on your mac, but it is an openly available model built for long-horizon work and also our most popular model on Ollama right now. GLM-5.2 on Ollama.

I don’t think the point is that every capable open model needs to run locally. The more interesting thing is that more people will put both large and small open models into the same harnesses they already use.

Sometimes that works. Sometimes the model completely loses the plot, fails tool calls, or cannot continue after compaction (if it compacts at all). It is tempting to call that a model problem.
